intro: Every day you meet messages built to change your mind. Some come from friends, teachers or trusted news outlets. Others come from people who want your anger, your vote, your money or your loyalty. In the twentieth century, governments on the far left and the far right learned to use posters, radio and film to shape the beliefs of whole nations. Democracies at war used propaganda too. Today the same tools travel through phones and feeds.

This unit has two parts. First you will learn to name the tools of propaganda: the enemy image, the big lie, the cult of personality, fear and the bandwagon. You will compare Soviet and Nazi posters and practice the checking habits that professional fact-checkers use. Then you will study how people are drawn into extremist movements on both extremes, what political violence has cost in Italy, Germany, Peru and Rwanda, and how communities and democracies push back.

By the end you will be able to take apart a persuasive message, check a claim before you share it, recognize warning signs in language and movements, and explain what makes civic life strong. You will also practice one of the most useful skills a citizen can have: disagreeing well with people who see the world differently.
bigQuestion: How can citizens recognize manipulation and extremism, and what keeps a free society strong against them?

timeline.t: The U.S. creates the Committee on Public Information to build support for World War I
Hitler's Mein Kampf describes the big lie while accusing others of it
Joseph Goebbels becomes Nazi minister of propaganda
The Institute for Propaganda Analysis publishes guides naming common devices
The UN adopts the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the Genocide Convention
Khrushchev's Secret Speech condemns Stalin's cult of personality
The Red Brigades kidnap and kill Aldo Moro in Italy
The Shining Path begins its war in Peru
Genocide in Rwanda follows months of dehumanizing radio broadcasts
EXIT-Deutschland begins helping people leave the far right
Peru's Truth and Reconciliation Commission issues its final report
A Science study finds false news spreads farther and faster online than true news

words.d: organized, one-sided communication meant to shape what large numbers of people believe or do
a picture of a whole group as one dangerous, often inhuman threat
a huge falsehood repeated so boldly and often that people come to believe it
propaganda presenting a living leader as a nearly perfect figure beyond criticism
a technique that urges people to join because everyone else supposedly has
checking a source by leaving it and seeing what other trusted sources say about it
a space where people mostly hear their own views repeated back to them
false information spread on purpose to mislead
a feeling of having been wronged or treated unfairly
describing people as less than human, such as animals, insects or disease
the groups people form outside government and business, such as congregations, clubs and charities
the principle that the same laws apply to everyone, including those in power

choices: Any message sent by a government
A news report with a small error
Organized, one-sided communication meant to shape mass opinion
test.why: Propaganda is organized, one-sided and aimed at large audiences.

test.q: Why did Soviet and Nazi posters look alike?
choices: They were drawn by the same artists
They were both made for elections in democracies
They used the same persuasion techniques for opposite ideas
test.why: Heroic leaders, united crowds and enemies appeared in both.

test.q: The stab-in-the-back myth is an example of
choices: a big lie repeated for years
test.why: It falsely blamed Germany's World War I defeat on traitors at home.

test.q: What did Khrushchev's Secret Speech condemn?
choices: The U.S. Office of War Information
test.why: In 1956 Khrushchev criticized the cult around Stalin.

test.q: The removal of about 120,000 Japanese Americans to camps shows that
choices: democracies at war can also feed prejudice
test.why: Wartime images and fear helped justify the camps; the U.S. apologized in 1988.

test.q: Which habit did professional fact-checkers use in the 2017 Stanford study?
test.why: They left the site to see what other sources said about it.

test.q: What do the four SIFT moves help a reader do?
choices: Check a claim before sharing it
test.why: Stop, Investigate, Find better coverage and Trace help slow false claims.

test.q: What did the 2018 Science study find about false news on Twitter?
choices: It spread more slowly than true news
It spread farther and faster than true news
It was spread mainly by bots
test.why: False news was about 70 percent more likely to be retweeted, mostly by people.

test.q: The Reichstag seat numbers from 1928 to 1932 show that
choices: the Nazis lost seats every year
both the far right and the far left grew during the Depression
test.why: Nazi seats rose from 12 to 230 and Communist seats from 54 to 89.

Listening to an opponent's best argument
Dividing people into a wholly good side and a wholly evil side
test.why: It leaves no room for neutral people or compromise.

test.q: RTLM radio in Rwanda is an example of
test.why: It called Tutsi cockroaches and urged violence; its leaders were convicted in 2003.

test.q: Which group was a far-right cell that murdered ten people in Germany?
test.why: The NSU committed the murders between 2000 and 2007.

test.q: What did Tocqueville praise in American life?
test.why: He saw associations as a school of self-government.

test.q: What helps most when someone tries to leave an extremist group?
choices: Being cut off by everyone they know
Keeping the decision secret from all adults
A new place to belong and people who believe they can change
test.why: Experts agree isolation makes leaving harder.

It proves one side is always right
test.why: Disagreeing well keeps disputes inside peaceful institutions.

write.prompt: Which matters more for protecting a democracy from extremism: individual habits, such as checking claims and disagreeing well, or strong institutions, such as a free press, fair courts and civic groups? Make a claim, support it with at least three facts or sources from this unit, and answer the strongest counterargument.
tips: Name your sources, such as the Stanford study, Peru's truth commission or the Reichstag seat numbers.
Use examples from both the far left and the far right.
Steelman the other side before you answer it.
Use unit terms like rule of law, civil society and dehumanization.
End by explaining why your evidence supports your claim.
